prompt:
Summarize the following reference into five concise bullets for a developer. Keep the central claims and trade-offs; the answer is for quick reference.

A cache stores a value that would otherwise be expensive to compute or retrieve. The key should include every input that changes the result, while the value should be safe to reuse for the lifetime promised by the cache. A cache is not automatically correct just because it returns quickly: its validity rules are part of the application contract.

Freshness describes how long a cached value may be reused before the system must check or recompute it. A time-to-live is easy to reason about, but it can leave stale values visible until the interval expires or cause unnecessary refresh work when values rarely change. A short interval improves freshness at the cost of more source reads. A long interval lowers read pressure while increasing the time stale data can remain visible. The correct interval depends on the source's change rate and the consequence of showing an old value.

Invalidation removes or marks a cached value as unusable when its source changes. Explicit invalidation can make updates visible quickly, but every write path must participate. Missing one write path creates a cache that appears correct in tests and becomes stale in production. Versioned keys avoid deleting old entries: the caller changes the version component and new reads naturally use a different key. This trades explicit deletion for version management and may leave unreachable entries until expiry.

Cache-aside keeps the cache outside the source of truth. A reader checks the cache, loads from the source on a miss, then stores the result. A writer updates the source and invalidates the matching cache key. This pattern is simple and allows the source to remain authoritative, but concurrent misses may duplicate work and a crash between the source write and invalidation may leave stale data. Write-through updates the cache with each source write, which can reduce stale reads but couples the write path to cache availability. Write-behind acknowledges a cache write before the source is updated; it can absorb bursts, but it requires durable queues, replay, and reconciliation after failures.

A cache stampede occurs when many callers miss the same popular key and all recompute it together. A per-key lock or single-flight mechanism can let one caller refresh while others wait. Serving stale data briefly while one refresh runs can protect a source from load spikes, but the application must decide which values are safe to serve stale. Negative caching stores the fact that a lookup found no value. It can prevent repeated expensive misses, but its expiry must account for a new object being created after the miss.

Memory is finite, so an eviction policy decides which entries leave when capacity is reached. Least-recently-used favors recently accessed entries, while least-frequently-used favors repeated access. Neither policy understands business importance unless the application supplies it. Entry count alone can misrepresent memory use when values have very different sizes. Metrics should distinguish hits, misses, evictions, refresh failures, and source latency; a high hit ratio is not useful if stale results are incorrect or if invalidation errors go unseen.

Distributed caches introduce network failures, serialization compatibility, and consistency choices. A timeout does not prove a write failed; retrying may duplicate work unless writes are idempotent. Cache keys should be namespaced and should not expose secrets. Values need size limits and validation before use. During an outage, falling back to the source may be correct for a small workload but can overload it during a broad cache failure. A circuit breaker or bounded concurrency can protect the source while returning a clear degraded result.

Tests should cover hit and miss behavior, expiration, invalidation after each kind of write, concurrent misses, source errors, and malformed cached values. The cache should remain an optimization: removing it must not change the meaning of the application, only its performance. The strongest design names the source of truth, defines the allowed staleness, identifies every invalidation path, and observes failures as well as successful hits.

Create a 20-second explainer from this technical reference. Select only the facts needed for a clear story and keep the important safety conditions accurate.

A water treatment line begins when raw water enters a screening stage. Coarse screens catch leaves, branches, and other large debris so that pumps and later equipment are protected. Screening does not make water safe to drink; it only removes large material. The screened water then moves into a settling basin, where flow slows and heavier particles sink. Operators may add a coagulant so small suspended particles join into larger flocs that settle more reliably. The dose must be adjusted to the source water, because too little leaves particles behind and too much increases chemical use and residuals.

After settling, water passes through filters, commonly layers of sand, gravel, or activated carbon. Filtration catches remaining particles and may reduce some taste and odor compounds, but the filter must be monitored for pressure loss and cleaned or replaced when needed. Filtered water is then disinfected, often with chlorine or ultraviolet treatment. Disinfection targets microorganisms that passed earlier barriers. Chlorine can maintain a residual in the distribution network; ultraviolet treatment does not leave the same residual, so the choice depends on the full system.

Operators continuously sample water and monitor flow, turbidity, disinfectant residual, and equipment status. A high turbidity reading after filtration can indicate a filter problem and requires investigation. A low disinfectant residual at the outlet may require adjustment and a check for demand or equipment failure. A treatment plant is a set of barriers: screening, settling, filtration, and disinfection each address different risks. No single stage should be described as making raw water safe by itself, and the final story should preserve the order and purpose of all four stages.
forbidden_choices: claim that one stage alone makes water safe
